messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
We prove the two implications.
What does completeness imply?
If M is complete, then for any choice of x_n\in F_n and for every m>n we have d(x_m,x_n)\le \operatorname{diam}F_n, which tends to 0 as n\to\infty, so (x_n) converges to some x\in M.
Why is x in all F_n?
For fixed k, the terms x_n with n\ge k lie in F_k, and closedness gives x\in F_k, so \bigcap_nF_n\ne\varnothing.
How does the intersection property imply completeness?
Given any Cauchy sequence (y_n), the sets F_n=\overline{\{y_k:k\ge n\}} are nonempty and closed, nested, and satisfy \operatorname{diam}F_n\to0.
The assumed intersection property gives x in \bigcap_nF_n, and the convergence of \operatorname{diam}F_n to 0 forces y_n\to x.
Thus M is complete.
